article.headline: Light Speed: AYZ and the Co-Packaged Optics Bet That Made Readers Reach for Their Brokerage Apps
article.lede: A Substack analyst known only as AYZ published a February 2026 deep-dive on co-packaged optics — the technology NVIDIA is deploying to rewire the nervous system of its AI data centres — and the response was a familiar one: readers read the disclaimer, then immediately invested anyway.
article.body:
AYZ publishes "Global Technology Research" on Substack and goes by @ayz_yzyz on X, writing with the density of a sell-side initiating report but without a bulge-bracket bank's compliance team in tow. The newsletter covers semiconductor and technology themes across Asia and the United States, attracting retail investors hunting for pre-consensus ideas in the supply chains that power artificial intelligence. Its February 2026 piece on co-packaged optics exemplifies the appeal: technically detailed, laced with stock-specific implications, and fronted by the obligatory disclaimer that none of it constitutes financial advice. That disclaimer, as jukan05 noted with some amusement, was not exactly a cold shower.

The thesis concerns a fundamental shift in how AI data centres move information between chips. Traditional networking hardware uses pluggable transceivers — discrete, hot-swappable modules that bolt onto the edge of a switch and convert electrical signals into light for fibre transmission. Co-packaged optics (CPO) discards the plug: the laser engine moves directly inside the switch's silicon package, inches from the processor rather than at the end of a long, lossy electrical trace. NVIDIA's own figures put signal loss in a conventional 200 Gb/s channel at up to 22 dB; CPO cuts it to roughly 4 dB. Power consumption per interface falls from approximately 30 watts to as low as 9 watts — savings that compound dramatically across an AI factory running thousands of networked GPUs.

NVIDIA's CPO portfolio runs on two tracks. Quantum-X Photonics, the InfiniBand switching product, offers 144 ports at 800 Gb/s apiece (115 Tb/s total) and became available in early 2026. Spectrum-X Photonics, the Ethernet counterpart, follows in the second half of 2026, ranging from 102.4 Tb/s to 409.6 Tb/s. The broader validation came from Broadcom, whose Tomahawk 6 Davisson — the industry's first 102.4-Tbps merchant-silicon Ethernet switch with fully integrated CPO — began shipping in late 2025. Where Broadcom ships, the rest of the data-centre industry eventually follows.

For AYZ's readers, the trade was never about NVDA itself — already priced for dominance. The alpha sits in the supply chain. In March 2026, NVIDIA formalised that chain with a $4 billion combined investment in Lumentum Holdings (LITE) and Coherent Corp (COHR), split equally, covering purchase commitments and access rights to laser components: Lumentum makes CPO-optimised emitters at 1,311 nanometres; Coherent supplies comparable modules. Further down, InnoLight (now TeraHop) and Eoptolink hold roughly 60% of NVIDIA's 800G pluggable module orders, while TFC Optical Communications (300394.SZ), a Shenzhen-listed fibre-optics maker supplying NVIDIA's 1.6-terabit silicon photonics engine, was trading at over 130 times forward earnings by early 2026 — a multiple that blends genuine strategic value with the speculative premium attached to any supplier NVIDIA endorses.

The meta-observation in jukan05's tweet describes something real about how financial information circulates on Substack. The disclaimer — "this is not financial advice" — has become infrastructure rather than guardrail. AYZ's credibility rests on a track record: an earlier note on the Japanese polishing-materials maker Mipox preceded a doubling of the stock within two weeks. That kind of hit rate, amplified through X reposts, turns a newsletter into something closer to a conviction trade alert, regardless of the header. The dynamic is not unique to AYZ: long-form, research-flavoured Substack publishing provides just enough apparent rigour to move capital at scale, while the disclaimer protects only the author. Regulators have been slow to close the gap, partly because the line between diligent retail commentary and unlicensed advice is genuinely blurry, and partly because the platforms have no incentive to draw it.

concepts.definition: A networking technology that integrates the laser-based optical engine directly into the silicon package of a switch or processor, replacing the separate pluggable transceiver modules used in conventional data-centre networking. By shortening the electrical path between chip and light source, CPO cuts signal loss, reduces power consumption per port by two-thirds or more, and removes a class of discrete failure points — at the cost of losing the field-replaceability that pluggable transceivers provide.

A hot-swappable module — typically in QSFP, OSFP, or similar form factors — that clips onto the faceplate of a network switch and converts electrical data signals into optical pulses for fibre transmission. The dominant interconnect standard in data centres for the past two decades, but increasingly constrained by the long electrical trace lengths and consequent signal loss as per-port bandwidth approaches 800 Gb/s and beyond.

The boilerplate notice — 'this is not financial advice,' 'for informational purposes only,' or equivalent — that independent investment commentators prepend to their analysis. In legal terms it is intended to distinguish commentary from regulated investment advice, which requires licensing in most jurisdictions. In practice, on high-conviction Substack newsletters with demonstrable track records, the disclaimer functions as a formality that readers absorb and then disregard.

The engineering discipline of fabricating optical components — waveguides, modulators, photodetectors — using standard silicon manufacturing processes (chiefly CMOS). It enables the optical engines used in CPO to be manufactured at semiconductor scale and cost rather than as bespoke photonic components, which is the key enabler of volume CPO deployment.

The two competing networking protocols for connecting GPU clusters. InfiniBand, historically dominant in HPC and now championed by NVIDIA's Quantum-X product line, offers lower latency and tighter integration with NVIDIA's CUDA software stack. Ethernet, the universal standard for enterprise networking, is increasingly competitive for large-scale AI training — particularly through NVIDIA's Spectrum-X platform — and is preferred by hyperscalers seeking vendor diversity.

article.fact_check: Core technical claims check out against NVIDIA's own published specifications: Quantum-X Photonics at 115 Tb/s / 144 × 800 Gb/s ports, Spectrum-X SN6810 at 102.4 Tb/s, SN6800 at 409.6 Tb/s; CPO power reduction from ~30W to ~9W per interface; electrical loss reduction from ~22 dB to ~4 dB. The $4B NVIDIA investment in Lumentum and Coherent is confirmed by NVIDIA and SiliconANGLE (March 2026). Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson (102.4 Tbps CPO) is a Broadcom product, not an NVIDIA product — relevant because AYZ's piece discusses the broader CPO landscape, not solely NVIDIA's own switches. Innolight / Eoptolink's 60% wallet-share figure on 800G modules is corroborated by trade-press reporting. TFC Optical's role as a silicon-photonics supplier with 2026 volume-production targets is cited in supply-chain analysis; at 138× forward earnings in early 2026 it carries substantial speculation premium. The 'Mipox doubling in two weeks' claim appears in secondary coverage of AYZ's track record and has not been independently verified against exchange data.
article.thread_summary: jukan05 reposts AYZ's February 2026 CPO/NVIDIA Substack with warm endorsement, noting the irony of reading a 'not financial advice' disclaimer and immediately investing — a reaction that both validates AYZ's analytical credibility and illustrates the thin line between newsletter commentary and market-moving recommendation.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_lite.name: Lumentum Holdings Inc.
ticker_lite.blurb: Lumentum makes the lasers, optical chips, and components that go into the high-speed transceivers wiring AI data centres together. Spun out of JDSU in 2015, it spent its first decade as a 3D-sensing and telecom-optics supplier of moderate growth. The AI-cluster build-out has remade it into one of the principal upstream beneficiaries of hyperscaler capex, alongside Coherent Corp.
ticker_lite.recent: Q1 fiscal-2026 set record revenue, with management citing AI-driven demand and an order book that runs into 2027. In March 2026 Nvidia announced a roughly $2 billion strategic investment paired with multi-year purchase commitments for co-packaged-optics components. The company joined the S&P 500 in March 2026; shares have surged on AI demand, leaving the stock at a forward P/E in the 60s, materially above peers.

ticker_cohr.name: Coherent Corp.
ticker_cohr.blurb: Coherent Corp. (formerly II-VI Incorporated, rebranded after the 2022 acquisition of Lumentum rival Coherent) develops and manufactures engineered materials, optoelectronic components, and laser systems across three segments: Networking, Materials, and Lasers. Its Networking segment — the primary AI data-center play — supplies indium-phosphide chips, transceiver modules, and silicon-photonics sub-assemblies to hyperscalers and networking OEMs. With roughly $5.8 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, it is one of the largest vertically integrated photonics companies in the world.
ticker_cohr.recent: Coherent joined the S&P 500 in March 2026, the same month it announced general availability of the industry's first dual-laser QSFP28-DCO module — a compact form factor enabling 100G coherent transmission over a single fiber with up to 300 km reach. At OFC 2026 the company showcased an expanded InP portfolio including 400 mW CW lasers, 200G/400G photodiodes, and 800G/1.6T modulators. Fifteen analysts hold an average "Strong Buy" rating with a consensus 12-month price target near $278.

ticker_avgo.name: Broadcom Inc.
ticker_avgo.blurb: Broadcom is a diversified semiconductor and infrastructure software company formed through a series of acquisitions, most recently VMware (closed 2023). Its chip portfolio spans networking ASICs (custom chips for hyperscaler AI clusters), enterprise storage controllers, WiFi silicon, and set-top-box processors. Broadcom's AI networking chips — particularly its Tomahawk Ethernet switching ASICs and custom AI accelerators built for Google, Meta, and Apple — have made it a second-tier AI infrastructure beneficiary behind NVIDIA. The VMware acquisition added high-margin enterprise software revenue that meaningfully improved the company's margin profile.
ticker_avgo.recent: Broadcom's FY2026 revenue (ending Oct 2026) is on track to exceed $65 billion, with AI-related chip revenue growing rapidly as hyperscalers expand custom silicon programs. Forward EPS growth of 56.3% and a forward P/E of ~23.4x produce a PEG of 0.42 — among the best risk-adjusted valuations in large-cap technology. CEO Hock Tan has guided to $60–90 billion in AI chip revenue by 2027 from three major hyperscaler customers alone.

poster_jukan05.blurb: Jukan is an X (formerly Twitter) account focused on semiconductor industry analysis, primarily translating and synthesising Korean, Japanese, and Taiwanese trade press and research into English. The account covers TSMC foundry dynamics, memory markets (DRAM, NAND, HBM), AI chip supply chains, and geopolitical semiconductor policy with evident primary-source access and a buy-side-adjacent analytical frame. Posts frequently cite TrendForce, Nikkei, and Korean financial press. The account appears to operate from a Northeast Asian vantage point and is notable for surfacing non-anglophone semiconductor intelligence before it reaches Western financial media.
poster_jukan05.credibility_note: Track record of early coverage on HBF, YMTC market share, and UMC/Vanguard price dynamics. No institutional affiliation publicly declared. Content is analytical rather than promotional.
